His heart fails. It's his sacrifice, and it's written to be the final line of the entire story — not a twist, not a rescue. What makes it land isn't spectacle. It's the peace that follows it, in contrast to everything chaotic that came before.

After the Reset, the survivors' minds are altered by what passed through them, and the horror of everything that came before gets remembered — not lied about, genuinely remembered — as scripture instead of history. Aegis becomes a figure called the Light Bringer, his old hard-light barriers romanticized into halos. The old glass towers fuse with living systems, vines and bioluminescent fungi threading through the same buildings that used to be sterile monuments to the people who caused all of this. That's the world the story eventually arrives at — the Epic of Altrulan, the myth that grows out of the wreckage of everything you've just heard.

None of that back half is written yet in full scene. What you've just heard — the river, the hospital, the lattice and the cage and the thing that has no fixed shape, the cohort in Sky Room, the arena, the printer, the mirror, the ceremony, the bunker — is everything that currently exists as finished narrative. Everything past 2228 for Dr. Tox, and everything past that first deployment for Aegis, is architecture waiting to be filled in. And somewhere out there, walking around with no memory of who he used to be, is a man named Rolan, cybernetically rebuilt, standing across a battlefield from the person who once beat him to death with his bare hands — and neither of them yet knows it. Carmy is out there too, rebuilt the same way, under a name that isn't hers anymore, and nothing has been written yet about whether her own death — betrayed by the man she loved, rather than refusing the program the way Cally did — left the same kind of crack in her, or a different one, or none at all.

That's the story so far.

Told once, straight through, the way it happened rather than the way it's filed.

Three people made by the same hand are out there right now, none of them aware of how close their threads already run to each other. Dr. Tox hunts the organization that built all of them, not knowing yet that two of its other products crossed his path years before he had a name for either one. Aegis serves an institution that has never once told him the truth about the four children it took from Sky Room, and stands in the field beside a man he already killed once, with no memory of either fact. Catalyst walks around loyal to a program that manufactured her hatred of it, unaware the hatred survived the very redirect meant to erase it. None of them know what the reader now does. That gap — between what the story's people understand and what the story itself has already shown — is where everything still to come is going to happen. The river, the arena, and the bunker were only ever the beginning of it.

But somewhere underneath that belief, in the part of her nobody knew was still there to redirect, something that used to be a girl in a room painted with a fake sky is still refusing to kill her own. Still waiting for a floor to split. Still furious — at the program, at the room, at every hand that has ever moved her without asking.

It won't surface on command. It won't surface soon.

It's worth being exact about what that means, because it isn't sentiment and it isn't memory in any form a scan could ever flag. Her wipe is as total as his — she doesn't consciously know the name Cally any better than Reese knows his own cohort's names, doesn't remember Carmy's face or the sound of Rolan's voice or a single hour of Sky Room. What survived isn't a person's grief. It's the shape a refusal leaves behind after everything else about the person who refused has been erased — a hatred of the State printed into her at the exact same layer as her obedience, so tangled with it that pulling one thread out would have unraveled both.

The bunker Alexander falls into doesn't announce itself as a grave. That's the first thing he notices — no warning signage, no biohazard glyphs, nothing his training has taught him to fear. Just a service door under eleven meters of dead earth, rated for a chemical storage facility that stopped existing on paper thirty years ago.

The air past the threshold is too clean. Filtered, recycled, still running on a budget somebody never stopped paying.

He follows the humming.

The room at the end of the corridor isn't a lab. It's a nursery wearing a lab's face — vat-lined walls, soft blue emergency light, the kind of quiet that hospitals manufacture on purpose. At the center of it, a column of matte black housing rises from floor to ceiling, veined with fiber conduit pulsing in a slow, patient rhythm. A printer. Not for plastic. Not for metal.

The plaque bolted to its base is small enough that he has to get close to read it.

The floor tells him otherwise — a tremor, low and mechanical, running up through the housing beside him like something enormous just took a breath.

The column splits down its seam with a sound like a held note finally exhaled. Vapor rolls out low across the floor, backlit blue, and inside the housing, something that used to be theory is standing upright in fluid, dark hair fanned weightless around a face built — not grown, built — to specification.

She isn't breathing yet. Then she is.

Her eyes open before the fluid finishes draining, which is wrong, which his forensic training flags immediately and his conscience refuses to let him file away as merely interesting. Someone matched the color on purpose.

"Cold," she says. First word. Not a scream, not confusion. An observation, delivered with the mild curiosity of someone reading a room for the first time and finding it slightly beneath her expectations.

She steps out onto the floor on legs that have never held weight and doesn't stumble. Doesn't even look like she considered stumbling as an option.

A brain in stasis isn't a person. It isn't nothing either, and that distinction turns out to be the entire, expensive problem of a project the engineers are calling, with a certain grim wit, Project Catalyst.

The first attempt to bring her back fails in eleven days. The printed body accepts the neural pattern, opens its eyes, and does nothing but scream — not fear, the engineers note with clinical irritation, but rage, undirected, aimed at the walls, the staff, itself. They terminate it before it can be calibrated and file it away as synaptic desync.

The next several attempts fail quieter. Catatonia. The pattern comes through too intact, too whole, and a whole person doesn't take direction well. She remembers too much — the arena, a friend's face, a promise made in a voice that wasn't really loving her at all — and the grief alone is enough to short the whole print out before it can even learn to walk.

Somewhere around the nineteenth attempt, someone in the division has an idea that will define every attempt after it.

What's known so far: his followers become chemically dependent on him first, then pass through something closer to religious ego dissolution, and finally arm themselves with resins drawn from his own lethal chemistry. Dependency, then surrender, then weaponization — the same three-step shape, over and over, in everyone who comes close enough to him to matter.

In 2236, that structure breaks. Dr. Tox loses control of his own cult — his followers' belief in him has outgrown anything he intended it to become — and the world enters what's called the Finale, four chaotic years that run through 2240. Every thread the story has been carrying — his, Aegis's, Catalyst's, the mega-cities, the wasteland — narrows across those four years toward one closing act.

That act is called the Bufadienolide Reset. Dr. Tox infiltrates the last standing corporate arcology, reaches its central hub, and overloads his own glands, flooding the city's life support with an aerosolized wave of the same chemistry that has defined his entire life.

A third has vanished entirely from ordinary sight, a cuttlefish-and-chameleon splice with total camouflage, and pays for it by needing to breathe through his own skin in water pure enough that anything else suffocates him. The last two are a pair, throats built to shatter concrete with sound, and every time they use it, their own bones take the same punishment the walls do. None of them asked to become what they are. All of them recognize, in the stranger who fell through their ceiling, someone who understands exactly what that costs. They help him escape.

Before he does, the archives give him what two years of pin boards and red string never could. His illness was never the plague. It never had anything to do with it. It was Subject CMXCIX's program — the same shut-down immunity experiment that took nine hundred and ninety-nine other children and gave the world nothing but him.

He finds his own file. He finds the other nine hundred and ninety-nine only as names.

"There it is," she says, soft, almost fond. "That's the look. I don't even know your name and I already know what you're worth to somebody."

Behind her, the terminal quietly appends one more line to a log that will never reach a review board. Cycle forty-one. Viability confirmed. Catalyst operational.

Alexander backs out of the room before she can say anything else. He doesn't run. He wants to.

He doesn't yet know the boy this was built to unmake. He will.

For now, she believes completely that she serves HOPE — the word she'll use for it, the same word Reese uses, for the same reason: neither of them has any information that would make them say it any other way. Whether that ever changes, whether some hour down the line she hears herself say the word RCC instead and doesn't understand why, isn't something the terminal in this room, or anyone who built it, has any way of predicting.

"You're not on the manifest," she says. Pleasant. Interested. Already working something out behind his face he can't see the shape of. "That's alright. I'm not particular about who watches me wake up." A small, private smile, aimed somewhere past his shoulder, like she's checking her reflection in glass that isn't there. "I'm told I'm very good at being watched."

He says nothing. His hand has found the doorframe without his permission, the way a body braces before it understands why.

"Do I have a name yet," she asks. Not what is my name — she already knows the file called her something once. She's asking what she's for now, which is, he'll understand much later, the only question this room ever actually taught her to ask.

He doesn't answer. She doesn't need him to. She's already reading it off him — the flinch he can't quite suppress, the half-second his eyes hold on her face too long — and something in her expression settles, satisfied, like a key finding its lock on the first try.

Underneath it, in smaller type, a secondary application — deployable against any high-value asset with a pre-existing attachment signature, recommended calibration period seventy-two hours — as if whatever she is could be re-aimed at anyone, given three days to learn the shape of a new person to hate.

Bond integrity. Like loyalty was a material property. Like the way a boy once looked at a girl in a concrete room painted with a fake sky was a specification the program could hit a number on and reproduce on demand.

Alexander doesn't know the name Aegis yet. Doesn't know it will matter. He only knows that whoever built this thing was proud enough of that number to leave it on a screen for anyone to find — and that everything about this room, the plaque, the readout, the corporate shorthand stamped into the housing, wears the same three letters he has spent two years learning to say instead of the ones people upstairs prefer. Not HOPE. RCC. The State. He has never once, in his life, called it anything gentler than what it is.

He should leave.

CHAPTER SEVEN — SNAKEHEAD

Cornered, eventually, by the facility's own security — because a man who falls through the ground into a restricted bunker doesn't get to leave quietly — Alexander finds an unlikely kind of help. The bunker isn't only a nursery for printed weapons. It's also a place where RCC's failed experiments were left to rot, and rot they did not do. What Alexander finds down there, beyond the Catalyst chamber, is a family — mutant, fiercely loyal to each other, and to nobody who built them. Four of them, each carrying a power and a cost bolted to the exact same source, the way his own toxin is both his weapon and his cage. One is half-toad, poison in the skin, capable of leaps that shouldn't be possible, and pays for it with a jaw that unhinges to drive a crushing, muscled tongue through anything in reach. Another is covered in pulsing translucent boils, able to flood a room with corrosive spray, and just as capable of turning that same acid against her own insides if the moment calls for it.

Project Catalyst, RCC Biosynth Division. Subject template, a designation he doesn't recognize yet. Status: cycle forty-one, gestation complete.

Forty. Forty prior cycles logged in the terminal beside it, each one a failure annotation in the same clipped corporate shorthand — rejection, synaptic desync, terminated pre-viability. Forty attempts to build a person who already existed once, and died, and apparently wasn't allowed to stay dead either time.

He shouldn't touch the terminal. He does anyway.

The screen wakes without asking for a password. It doesn't need to guard itself down here — nobody was ever supposed to find this room who wasn't already cleared to see it. He reads a functional profile he doesn't fully understand yet: targeted affective destabilization. A primary vector, listed by subject number, with a bond integrity logged at ninety-four point six percent.

Ask her, and she would deny any of it. Not lie — deny, sincerely, because she genuinely does not know.

She isn't the only one the arena gave back. Carmy didn't stay dead either. Recovered the same way, in the same building, on the same principle — a body reprinted around a harvested pattern, deployed under a different name than the one she died with. Whatever crack Cally's death-by-refusal left in her, Carmy's death-by-betrayal may or may not have left the same kind of seam in her. Nobody who built either of them has ever bothered to check.

That's where Project Catalyst's own internal logs end. What happened in the room the night she actually woke isn't written anywhere in RCC's archive, because nobody from RCC was in the room to see it. Someone else was — a man who had fallen through the ground two years and one week after walking out of a hospital, chasing a hunch that had nothing to do with any of this, and had wandered, without meaning to, into the one room in the facility that could have told him who Aegis really was, if he'd known to ask.

Don't erase the original pattern. Redirect it. Hatred is useful. Hatred is load-bearing, for a weapon built like this — so leave it intact, and just point it somewhere the program can use. Not at the people who built her. At whoever they hand her to.

On paper, it works. Attempt after attempt walks, talks, takes target profiles, executes exactly as specified. What the paper doesn't show is the residue — a thin thread of something underneath the compliance that nobody flags, because by the time anyone's running these later cycles, they've inherited the project long after anyone still knew what to look for. They call it noise. They call it acceptable variance. They sign off on deployment.

On the forty-first attempt, she wakes up viable. Operational. As far as any part of her that could report on the matter would say, she believes completely that she serves the people who built her.

He escapes with the help of the family the bunker made without meaning to, and he comes back later to claim the place as his own. By the time the fall from the hospital, the archive, the escape, and the return are finished, Alexander Balklin is gone in every way that matters, and what's left in his place is fully armored, fully armed, and based out of a fortress the world will come to call Snakehead. Everything about him by then — the black polymer and titanium, the amber vial he still fills by hand, the scarred forearm, the tank top folded away for a suit built entirely out of medical equipment turned to other purposes — has already been decided, years earlier, by a boy in a hospital room with nothing to do but figure himself out.

The date is 2228. The world calls him Dr. Tox.


CHAPTER EIGHT — WHAT'S COME SINCE, AND WHAT'S STILL COMING

This is where the fully-written story runs out, but not where it stops.

Between 2228 and 2236, Dr. Tox operates out of Snakehead and builds a following — a cult, in the most literal sense, bound to him by need before it's bound to him by belief.

A woman's voice, warm on purpose, the way a nurse's voice is warm on purpose. "Welcome back, Aegis."

The name lands on him like it's always been his. It hasn't. Nobody in the room corrects that, and nobody ever will.

They walk him to a mirror before they walk him anywhere else, and that's not an accident either — nothing on this floor is an accident. The reflection isn't quite the boy who went under. Taller. Denser through the shoulders in a way that took him a decade of trauma to build and took the enhancements four days to finish. Faint light under the skin at his wrists, dormant, waiting on a trigger nobody's told him about yet. New scarring threads up both forearms, fine and deliberate, the kind a surgeon leaves rather than a wound. Right now there's only a face that's unmistakably his, arranged into something the marketing team will later describe as approachable strength.

"You look like you're supposed to," the woman says, satisfied, like she's confirming a delivery. "That matters more than you'd think."

Twenty came out the other side of it, and of those twenty, the people running this ceremony have chosen to stand him up alone above a hundred thousand faces and call him the finest of them. Not first. Greatest. The distinction matters to whoever's writing his mythology — a first is an accident of order. A greatest is a verdict, one a crowd can love without ever having to ask about the other nineteen.

"Nineteen others walked this path beside him," the announcer says, voice pitched to carry over the swelling crowd, "and from among heroes, a hero rose highest. Elevated not by chance, but by strength, by loyalty, by sacrifice beyond what any of us could ask of a child." A pause, timed for the cameras. "Citizens of the Spire — I give you Aegis."

The sound that comes back at him stops being applause somewhere in the first second. It's a roar, tens of thousands of voices chanting a name shaped by mouths that have never met him, cheering for a boy who has no idea there were fifty-five trials before his own succeeded, that somewhere beneath their glass and skybridges a printer is quietly manufacturing a girl whose death made him what's standing on this platform right now.

Down the same corridor — same recycled air, same hum in the walls, same blue emergency light nobody ever bothered to warm — the boy who will wake up as Aegis is being walked into a chamber the staff will later call, in clipped internal shorthand, the long sleep. He doesn't know there's a second gurney two doors down. Nobody tells him. Nobody tells her either, not that she's in any state yet to be told anything.

Their files, if anyone had ever laid them side by side, would share a timestamp down to the minute. Two children, processed thirty meters apart, neither aware the other had survived the room at all. Whatever thread once ran between them gets filed under two separate case numbers, handled by two separate teams, and nobody in the program considers that a loss. To them it was never a thread. It was an inefficiency they'd already priced in.

His memory gets shaved down to almost nothing. Hers gets harvested whole. Different verbs for a similar theft.

By the metrics the program cares about, she's inventory.

The recovery team doesn't move like medics. They move like men collecting a sample that happens to still be warm. Full-spectrum neural preservation gives you a two-minute window if you're fast, four if you're willing to cut corners on the tissue, and the technician running point on this one has done it enough times that his hands don't shake anymore. He doesn't use her name. The manifest calls her RCC53-Delta-2, and that's the only handle he lets himself reach for, because the ones who use names start to hesitate, and hesitation costs the window.

The brain comes out intact. That's the only mercy in the room, and it isn't meant for her. Whatever the shot did to the rest of her, it never touched the one organ the program actually cared about. Her brain never died at all — not really, not in the way the manifest's timestamp implies. It only stopped, the way a held breath stops, waiting on a machine to remember how to let it go again.

He doesn't ask what he's supposed to look like for. He doesn't have the vocabulary yet to know that's the question that should worry him.

They don't tell him about the room he actually came from. They don't tell him about the floor that split, or a girl with a wound near her jaw, or the sound a body makes when you beat it long past the point where it stops being your friend. What they give him instead is smaller, cleaner, and fits in a single sentence, repeated by three different people in three different rooms until it starts to sound like something he thought of himself: you survived something terrible so you could protect people from it happening again.

It isn't a lie, exactly. It's a lie shaped like the exact hole the truth left behind, poured in while the wound was still open enough to take any shape they gave it. Something behind his eyes flinches at the word terrible — a flash with no picture attached, just pressure, just grief with the label torn off.

Carmy looked at Rolan across the seam, pleading, a fresh wound near her jaw already bleeding into a tear tracking down her face. Please, my love, she told him — they'd only ever had each other, all these years. If they all refused, maybe they could at least die together. One last kiss, she said, and laughed even through the pain of it, almost hopeful. And this time, she said, they wouldn't have to hide in the ceiling grates.

Rolan didn't refuse with the rest of them. He crossed the seam to her, arms wide, blade already vanished up his sleeve, and embraced her, kissed her, and drove that blade into her while he was still smiling, telling her — loud enough for the others to hear — that his love for her was real, that maybe he only loved himself, and thanking her for loving him too.

Cally saw it happen. Whatever was left of her composure went with it — devastation, raw and total, breaking across her face in the half-second before Reese saw it too.

"Orientation's this afternoon," someone tells him, already walking, already handing him a mission brief he never asked for. "Field deployment inside the week. You're a fast learner." A pause, almost kind. "You're going to save a lot of people, Aegis. Try to enjoy it. Not everyone gets to."

He doesn't ask what happened to the ones who didn't get to. He doesn't ask why the words not everyone made something in his chest go cold and quiet, fast, like a door closing somewhere he can't see.

He follows the tablet's directions down a hallway that looks like every other hallway in the building, and somewhere behind him, sealed off from anyone with his clearance, sits a room with a printer in it, cycling toward a version of a girl he no longer has a name for.

He walks the other way. He always will, for a long time yet — and for years, whenever he speaks of the people who made him what he is, he will call them by the only name they ever gave him for themselves. HOPE. Not RCC. Not the State.

Chosen and installed rather than engineered into him before birth, which marks him as something entirely outside HOPE's own catalogue.

What Aegis doesn't know — what nothing in his sim scores or his mission brief will ever tell him — is that the man sizing him up across the smoke and collapsed scaffolding is the same boy whose skull he caved in with his bare hands two years ago, on a floor that split beneath both of them. Neither of them remembers it. RCC saw to that on both sides, and whether that was mercy or simply cheaper than the alternative depends entirely on who you ask. His name, once, was Rolan. Nothing in this fight is going to remind either of them of that.

He clocks Reese before Reese is fully off the ramp. Doesn't stop moving. "New," he says, not quite a question, sizing him up across the wreckage like he's a line item being updated in real time. "They finally sent the amber-lit one down from the towers. I wondered when."

Reese doesn't know what to say to that.

His memory was taken apart and put back together with almost nothing left in it — nothing but Sky Room, the four of them playing on a mat under a painted sky, and one flash, without context, of the moment the other three stopped being alive.

He wouldn't remember their names. He wouldn't remember why any of it happened. He would only carry, for the rest of his life, an ache with no story attached to it, and a program more than willing to fill that silence in with whatever story served them best.


CHAPTER FIVE — THE MIRROR THEY HAND HIM

The lid doesn't open so much as it's unveiled — a hiss of pressure, a wash of light calibrated warm instead of clinical, because someone on this floor understood a long time ago that the first thing an asset sees sets the tone for everything that comes after. No fluorescent white. Amber. Gold-edged. Almost reverent.

He doesn't remember his own name yet. He remembers cold, and before that, a sound he can't place — high, broken, that might have been his own voice.

"There he is."

He beat Rolan to death with his bare hands. His best friend. He didn't remember deciding to do it. A single shot came down from above and killed Cally where she stood. The voice that had split the floor spoke one more time, flat, almost bored: they had broken the rules. They should have killed their own pair. Now they had no one.

What came after the arena wasn't punishment, at least not one anyone in the program would have called that. Reese went into cryo. Whatever enhancements the program had already embedded in him, dormant until then, would be activated on the other side of it.

He mistakes it for gratitude. That mistake will cost him for years.

They don't rush the next part underground. This part they want seen.

They take him up — past the checkpoints, past the filtered air, past the line where the world stops being concrete and starts being glass — into the Spire, one of the cities the elite never had to leave when everything else fell apart. Towers stitched together with skybridges and light. Air that costs money to breathe clean.

The plaza is already full when they walk him out onto the platform. Tens of thousands of people, real and holographic both, packed shoulder to shoulder under a canopy of screens broadcasting his face forty meters tall in every direction, softened, warmed, made kind by an editing suite that worked hard on it. He isn't the first — they don't hide that from him, because hiding it would rob them of a better story. Twenty children went into this trial.

He doesn't know the name Rolan, doesn't know what this man will come to mean to the next stretch of his life, doesn't know that this fight is the first thread that will eventually start pulling the amber lighting apart from the inside.

He only knows that when the man finally looks at him properly, something in his expression is doing quiet, careful arithmetic — the same way the crowd's chant did an hour ago, except his doesn't sound like it's already decided what the answer is.

"Try to keep up, hero," Rolan says, and turns back into the fight without waiting to see if he will.


CHAPTER SIX — CATALYST

She's declared dead at three-fourteen in the morning, by a clock nobody in the room particularly believes in. The shot took her from above, clean, and by every metric a soldier cares about, she's finished. No pulse. No motor response. Blood already cooling into the seam that split the arena floor beneath her — the same arena, the same night, the same floor that took Carmy and Rolan and left Reese standing over both of them with blood on his hands he wouldn't remember by morning.

He hasn't earned the second name yet, and won't, until something finally breaks that first one open.

His first deployment sends him down into the lower ring of the city, into what the brief calls a containment action against insurgent elements — the State's word for the people the plague left behind, fighting back with whatever the glass towers never bothered to take from them. He isn't alone on the ground for long.

There's already someone there when his transport sets down — mid-fight, unhurried in a way that unsettles Reese more than urgency would, moving through a knot of fighters like their weapons are a formality he's humoring rather than a threat he's managing. Where Reese's enhancements are dormant light under skin, this man's are visible from across the wreckage — plating at the joints, a faint mechanical whir under the motion of his arms, one eye replaced with something that catches the light wrong. Cybernetic, not grown.

Someone fastens an insignia to his chest before he's even finished deciding how it feels to be looked at like this.

He wants, with an intensity that surprises him, to be worthy of it. That want isn't manufactured. That's the cruelest part of the whole design — nobody had to build his need to matter, his need to be good, his need to make the deaths behind all that amber lighting mean something. They only had to make sure he never found out what those deaths actually were, and then let a good kid's own decency do the rest of the work for them.

There's no time built into his schedule to sit with any of this. That's deliberate too. Stillness is where the cracks show, and the people who built him have learned, across fifty-five trials and over a thousand deaths, that the fastest way to keep a crack from showing is to never let the asset stop moving long enough to feel it.

Nothing he wears or carries was chosen for how it looks. Matte black polymer over machined titanium plating. Medical-grade stainless and borosilicate glass in every fitting that matters. The surgical tubing that feeds his gauntlets runs on the outside of his gear rather than hidden beneath it, deliberately visible — the plumbing is the point, not something to be embarrassed about. The scab, once it's set, has the look of black lacquer or obsidian, cracking faintly at the joints where he has to bend, catching a thin green sheen if the light hits it wrong. His forearms carry more scarring than the rest of him combined, and none of it came from a fight. It's a record of self-injection, thousands of doses deep, the closest thing he has to a diary. There's no chrome anywhere on him. No gloss, no color for its own sake. If something on him shines, it's because it's wet, medical, or a wound — there's no fourth category.

There's a single idea underneath all of it, and it's the only idea that matters when you're trying to understand him.

Most of them believed, by then, that something better was waiting for them on the other side of all of it.

That belief was the actual product HOPE was manufacturing. And the program had, by the time any given trial reached its final year, a very specific solution for what to do with it.

Across fifty-five trials — fifty-three fully documented, two more held back for later — the program ran eleven hundred children through this exact structure. No trial produced more than two survivors, even before the final stage did its work. More than a thousand children never made it out the other side.

Trial fifty-three's fourth cohort was Reese, Cally, Carmy, and Rolan. By every internal metric the program kept, they were the closest bond in the entire trial, and the strongest performers on the floor. Reese had feelings for Cally that two years of shyness and a program that actively discouraged attachment never let him act on.

He doesn't remember what happened while he was gone. He wakes up and reads the aftermath the way he was trained to read any other crime scene — like evidence of something terrible that he wasn't there to witness, even though every drop of blood on his hands says otherwise.

There are two entirely different silhouettes a person could draw of him, and neither one is a lie. In the ordinary state, he reads as too thin to be dangerous — narrow, vertical, contained, a long neck and lean shoulders that carry no obvious bulk anywhere. Whatever threat he represents comes from stillness, not size. In the other state, nothing about him is symmetrical anymore. The horror isn't scale, it's wrongness — joints in numbers they shouldn't come in, shoulders sitting too high, a jaw that's outgrown the skull holding it. It never reads as strength. It reads as improvisation, because that's exactly what it is. And the moment between the two states is never clean.

Some accounts of him from that era add a long, heavy, desaturated green cape — whether it was ever really his, or a barrier he wore for the obvious reason that a man whose breath once killed a town has good cause to want distance from anyone standing near him, isn't something anyone's ever settled. At home — if Snakehead ever came to feel like home — he wore a plain white tank top, dark work trousers, a cigarette he rarely finished, and let the scars along his arm do whatever talking needed doing.

This was the man walking through the wasteland during those twelve months of reconnaissance. Not yet Dr. Tox. Not yet based anywhere. Just a former patient who had learned, the hard way, to trust his own body as a weapon before he trusted anyone else's protection.

He wasn't the only person that decade whose body had been turned into something else entirely without being asked. Two others were already living through it, in a much taller building, a long way from any hospital room.

CHAPTER FOUR — TRIAL FIFTY-THREE

Long before anyone called him Aegis, before the mirror and the ceremony and a crowd chanting a name he hadn't chosen for himself, there was a boy in a room painted to look like somewhere it wasn't.

RCC had built a second program alongside everything else it was running that decade, and this one wasn't about class weapons or population control. It was about manufacturing heroes — real ones, or at least ones the public would believe were real, engineered from the ground up to carry the backstory of a martyr and the loyalty of a weapon. Officially it stood for Health, Optimization, and Peak Evolution. Everyone inside it called it HOPE. The design thesis, if anyone had ever said it plainly to the people running it, was ugly in a way that would have ended careers: give them the tragedy of a villain and the conscience of whoever encoded them, then sell them to the public as saviors.

Each trial ran the same way.

The short-term shock of whatever's happening to him collides with something older, inherited, buried down in whatever the Amazonian program originally handed his ancestors' biology, and his intellect simply goes out like a light.

What happens after that isn't a transformation in any clean sense. His body stops obeying fixed rules the moment it decides survival matters more than cognition. It redraws itself on the fly, generating whatever it judges necessary to survive the immediate threat — a hormonal surge, growth hormone above all, letting it pack on dense, unnatural mass and alter bone density in seconds. There's no fixed shape to what comes out of him. Pale skin, stretched taut. Thick blackened veins, bulging, visibly pulsing. Eyes fully consumed by a sickly luminous green, no iris, no pupil left in them. A jaw distended past anything a human skull should allow. That much is constant. Everything else depends entirely on what's trying to kill him.

A cold, desaturated gray-teal is the world itself — concrete, corridors, daylight, the institutional indifference that put him in a hospital bed in the first place. His blood, once dried, reads as black shading into a near-black red, the color of fluid lines, blade channels, and dried plate. Clinical white belongs only to memory — the seventeen years, the sterile room, the plain tank top he still wears at home, because some part of him never fully left that room.

If you only ever knew three images of him, these would be enough to explain everything else. The first is the injection — shirtless in whatever passes for a medical bay wherever he's staying, scarred arm laid bare, a lead-shielded syringe in his other hand, jaw clenched, eyes shut, because the pain of it is absolute and also completely routine, a thing his body stopped being surprised by years ago. The second is the scab itself, seen close — a wound that isn't bleeding, sealed instead beneath a thick, glossy black plate that has visibly pulled the surrounding tissue inward to close itself.

The third is the aftermath: collapsed, human-shaped again, emaciated, his hands coated in blood he has no memory of spilling.

By the time he was walking privately owned facilities at night, breaking into places that had never expected a trespasser, he looked like this: pale to the point of near-bloodlessness, hollow through the cheeks, a long narrow jaw, cold pale gray-blue eyes that gave away nothing. A short dark buzzcut. Faint blue veining visible at his temples and throat if you knew to look for it. Tall, lean, built for endurance rather than power, every tendon visible under skin that never seemed to carry any spare weight. Heavy scarring ran the length of his right forearm, centered on a surgical shunt port that fed a line he kept close to his body out of old habit. In the field, eventually, that frame carried matte black tactical gear, segmented plating at the shoulders and forearms, two heavy throwing knives crossed in an X across his chest, a cluster of exposed syringe barrels mounted along one gauntlet.

Sustained gunfire gets overlapping plates of hardened scab across his chest and shoulders. A wall of shields or barricades gets grotesque overdevelopment through his arms, joints sitting wrong in their sockets. A target running from him gets elongated limbs, extra joints, a lean quadrupedal gait built purely for closing distance. A room full of bodies gets reach — arms and fingers longer than anything should be. It never generates the same shape twice. That unpredictability isn't a side effect. It's the entire nature of the thing.

What it costs him is everything that makes him dangerous in the ordinary sense. All of his grace, all of his precision, dissolves the moment this takes over — replaced by sloppy, reckless, unstoppable momentum that has no interest in being clever. And when it's finished, when whatever threat provoked it has been handled, he comes back to himself wrecked. Hollowed. Skeletal, skin loose over a frame that's been stripped of every reserve it had to draw on, sunken all the way down to the skull.

There's no glowing seam, no graceful unfolding. What people actually see is failure — his suit splitting at the load points, plating lifting away from straps that were never built to hold what's happening underneath them. The transformation isn't a reveal. It's a wardrobe malfunction with teeth.

He fights, on the days that state doesn't take him, with the cold calculation of a man who was trained as a scientist before he was trained as anything else. He doesn't aim for vital organs. He doesn't need to. Micro-dart gauntlets draw the poison directly from a shunt surgically set into his own wrist, feeding a manifold along the back of the glove. Throwing knives, hollowed down their centers, carry the same payload through a fill port at the base of the blade. Arrows do the same, glass-barreled heads standing in for broadheads. Even his own wounds are a weapon, once they've sealed — that black lacquered scab is lethal to anyone who forgets, even for a second, what it's made of.

Twenty lab-grown children, kept together from infancy to age five in a concrete holding block the staff called Sky Room — bunks along one wall, a play mat in the center, and a mural of a blue sky and green fields painted across the ceiling and walls, because somebody early in the program's history had decided children raised without a sky should at least be given the picture of one. At five, the twenty were split into five cohorts of four. From five to ten came years of physical, mental, and emotional training that wasn't accidental in its cruelty — near-death conditioning, deliberately traumatic, designed to break something in a child and rebuild it loyal to whoever did the rebuilding. At eleven, each cohort was made to fight to the death against incarcerated enemies of the State, so that killing stopped being theoretical. By twelve, whatever cohort survived that had usually been forged into something close to family — bound by fear, by loyalty, by the particular kind of brotherhood that only gets built inside a shared atrocity.

Cally and Carmy had been friends since Sky Room, before either of them understood what the mural on the ceiling was covering for. Rolan was the odd one — reckless, always the reason the four of them got in trouble, and also, by a wide margin, the top prospect among them, which made the others forgive almost everything else about him.

It was Cally who found out what the final stage actually was. Buried in a maintenance terminal she wasn't supposed to have access to, a protocol confirming what none of the staff had ever said aloud: every surviving cohort would eventually be brought down to its final four, and reduced by half again, until only the strongest of the strong were left standing. She told the other three. Three of them were horrified. Rolan wasn't.

The arena, when it came, split its floor beneath all four of them at once. A voice from somewhere above told them only two could remain. Reese was set against Cally. Carmy was set against Rolan.

The three who loved each other threw their weapons down together, refusing the choice outright.

Medicine as violence. Containment as identity. Every object in his life is a piece of medical equipment doing something a piece of medical equipment was never built to do. Nothing about him is decorative. Nothing about him is meant to look heroic. If it wouldn't exist in a hospital, and it hasn't been turned against its own purpose, it doesn't belong anywhere near him.

Even the way he reads is medical. Amber means contained — the vial, the cage, the version of himself he can still trust to make decisions. Sickly green means loose — the toxin unbound, the state where he stops being anyone in particular. The two colors never share equal weight in the same frame. When green starts winning, he's losing, and anyone who's spent enough time around him learns to read that shift before he says a word. The rest of his palette carries meaning too, quieter but just as fixed.

Whether every transformation his body is capable of burns down a piece of that supply — whether the amber vial is a finite thing he has to keep replenishing by hand, on a clock only he understands — is something even the people who know him best still argue about. He has never said.

His blood doesn't clot the way an ordinary wound closes, either. Exposed to open air, it dries the way acrylic paint dries — fast, violent, pulling the surrounding tissue together as it hardens, sealing whatever's underneath beneath a black lacquered plate. It looks, to anyone watching for the first time, like armor growing directly out of a wound. It is armor. And it stays lethal to touch for exactly as long as the fluid underneath stays wet.

All of that is what he lives with on an ordinary day. It isn't the worst of what he carries.

Severe trauma does something to him that nothing else does. An extreme adrenaline spike accelerates his heart rate past the point his body can regulate, thinning the wall between blood and brain, and when that wall gives, toxic blood floods in — and something in the collision short-circuits him entirely.

Two years and one week after he walked out of that hospital, mid-trek, chasing a lead that felt like every other lead he'd chased for a year, the ground gave out beneath him. He fell through a cavern into something built to stay hidden — a reinforced bunker, deep under the earth, that hadn't expected visitors.

Before that fall, though — before the cavern, before the bunker, before he had any name but his own — it's worth pausing on exactly what those twelve months of reconnaissance were carried out by. Not a man with powers, in any way the world would come to understand that word once it met him. A man who had spent two years turning a diagnosis into a discipline, the same patient, forensic way he'd once turned a hospital room into a doctorate.


CHAPTER THREE — THE MAN AND THE THING THAT KEEPS HIM ALIVE

There's a version of Alexander that any casual observer could sum up in a sentence, and it wouldn't tell them anything true.

It became poison — immediate, lethal, carried through every vessel in his body — and his own antibodies, unable to accept containment, spent every waking hour trying to escape through his skin, through his sweat, through the air he breathed out. The plain fact of being alive made him a biological hazard to anyone who shared a room with him for more than a few minutes. That's what those seventeen years in isolation actually were. Not overcaution. Necessity.

At fifteen, in that same hospital bed, he built the only thing that made any of it survivable. A radioactive medication, volatile and precisely dosed, that forces his own hyperaggressive immune system to turn inward instead of out — trapping the antibodies deep in his veins instead of letting them find a door. It isn't a cure. It was never meant to be one. It's a cage he designed for himself because there was no one else left who was going to build it for him, and for the rest of his life, he will be the only person alive who knows how to make more of it.

There is a third category, separate from either of these, and it matters more than anything else in this story, because it's the one that produced the man this whole thing is really about. Before the plague. Before HOPE. Before any of the class architecture that would come to define the world, RCC ran a much smaller, much older program — one that had nothing to do with class weapons or population control. It was about something more private than that. It was about whether death itself could be beaten.

That program only ever produced one real success. This is his story, and it starts a long time before he had a name people would come to fear. It runs alongside two other stories — a boy the same program's sister project would come to call a hero, and a girl that project killed once and then refused to let stay dead. All three of them start, in their own way, in the same decade, under the same hand, and none of them know about the other two yet.

DR. TOX: AGE OF GLASS AND GREED

The Story So Far — Revised Edition

A note before you start: this isn't the reference bible. It's everything currently written, told in order, as one continuous story. A few threads near the end are still open questions rather than settled fact, and you'll feel where the story goes quiet and turns back into notes — that's intentional. This is where the telling currently stops, not where it ends.

PROLOGUE — THE WORLD THAT LET THIS HAPPEN

It starts around the year you're living in now. Not with an asteroid, not with a war. With greed, the ordinary kind, given two hundred years and nothing in its way.

A civilization with every reason to advance instead regresses everywhere except the one narrow channel that protects the people already in power. Technology doesn't climb. It gets funneled entirely toward whatever problem the last round of greed created, and nothing else. So the world you'd expect from an era this far ahead never arrives.

They called him Subject CMXCIX. Nine hundred and ninety-nine of one thousand. His name was Alexander.

By every metric that mattered to the people running the study, the program was a catastrophic failure — one semi-success against nine hundred ninety-nine losses — and so they shut it down. Alexander was the only piece of it they left alive.

What survived in him wasn't the plague. It would take him decades to understand that distinction, but it's true from this moment forward: what happened to Alexander in that river is a different animal entirely from the disease that would one day split the whole world into two classes. His cells had abandoned the ordinary double helix and rebuilt themselves into something else — a fortified lattice structure that made cellular death and cellular breakdown functionally impossible. He couldn't get sick. He couldn't decay.

CHAPTER ONE — THE RIVER

There's a small town in Idaho that doesn't exist on any map that matters anymore, and there's a reason for that.

RCC had been studying an isolated tribe in the Amazon, people who'd achieved something close to functional biological immortality through generations of exposure to a single species of poison toad. Whatever they'd found there, the company wanted it synthesized, and wanted it tested somewhere nobody would ask questions. So they dumped an engineered biohazard into a small town's river and let it pass as an environmental contamination event. A tragedy. An accident. The kind of thing that makes the news for a week and then doesn't.

One thousand children passed through that study. The town died around them, quietly, the way towns die when nobody outside them is watching. And when it was finished, when the program's own doctors added up the results, there was exactly one child left who had survived it in any form that counted as success.

RCC built the heroes too — Project HOPE, the manufactured protectors, engineered from childhood to have the backstory of a martyr and the loyalty of a weapon. And only once its own class was immune, augmented, and safely behind glass did RCC release the plague. Not an accident. Not a natural outbreak. A weapon, engineered specifically to leave the unmodified population marked, suffering, and sorted into a class beneath the healthy.

That's the split the whole world lives inside now. Behind the glass, in the arcologies, the wealthy and the healthy — protected from a catastrophe they built with their own hands. Outside it, in the wasteland, the mutated and the suffering, marked by a disease they never had any say in receiving. The plague itself isn't a death sentence. It's worse than that. A curse mark. Purgatory instead of an ending. The body doesn't die from it — it just keeps dwindling, unraveling toward some evolution it never completes, for as long as the person carries it, which is usually the rest of their life.

He also couldn't touch another human being without killing them, because his blood carried the toxin as an active, lethal poison, and his body — desperate to purge what it had been given — tried to push the antibodies out through his sweat, his breath, anything that let them escape.

He spent the next seventeen-plus years of his life inside a sterile hospital room, fighting a war his own body had already half-lost, in complete isolation from the world outside the glass. It cost him his childhood. In exchange, it gave him something almost nobody else gets from that kind of solitude — an unbroken, unhurried, entirely undistracted intellect. There was nothing else to do in that room but think, and read, and eventually, understand his own condition better than the people who'd caused it ever had.

At fifteen years old, still inside that hospital room, he solved the one problem that had made his life livable at all. He engineered a volatile radioactive medication — a cage, not a cure — that forced his hyperaggressive immune system to work inward instead of out, trapping the antibodies deep in his veins where they couldn't reach anyone else.

It wasn't a power. It was containment, built by a child, because no one else was going to build it for him.

He walked out of that hospital at twenty-four years old with a doctorate in forensic medical science, specializing — inevitably — in biological anomalies. It was the year 2226. The same year, though he had no way of knowing it yet, that the rest of the world fell apart too.


CHAPTER TWO — THE REBUILDING

Seventeen years of bed rest doesn't leave a body ready for anything. The first six months out of that hospital were pure rehabilitation — nothing dramatic, nothing heroic, just the slow, exhausting work of teaching atrophied muscle how to be a body again.

The six months after that were different. He took up martial arts. Boxing. Mechanical engineering. Not as hobbies — as disciplines, deliberately chosen, the way a man chooses tools before he knows exactly what he's going to build with them.

By the end of that year he was trained, armed, and had started doing something he hadn't let himself do in the hospital: he'd started treating his own illness as a weapon instead of a wound.

And somewhere in that stretch, a thought started forming that wouldn't leave him alone. Someone had done this to him. It wasn't random. It wasn't an accident of geography or bad luck. Someone had made a decision, a long time ago, in a room he'd never see, and he had spent his entire childhood paying for it without knowing their name.

What started as hiking became something else almost immediately. He began breaking into privately owned, restricted facilities — chasing the hunch, following threads that shouldn't have connected to anything but somehow kept connecting to each other. Twelve months of it. Pin boards. Red string. Photographs of things that would look completely mundane to anyone who didn't already suspect what they were looking at. An obsession that had, without his really intending it, taken the shape of art.

They were never released as cures. They were self-administered upgrades, kept secret, given first to the exact people who would go on to unleash the thing those upgrades protected against.

Underneath that single sentence sit three separate branches of genetic manipulation, and they shouldn't be confused with each other even though they all trace back to the same building. The first is the plague itself — the class weapon, released only after the wealthy had already secured their own immunity. The second is a much older, much smaller program that predates everything else: true mutation, the kind that made one man in Idaho into something the plague never touched, for reasons that had nothing to do with class warfare. The third is newer still — synaptic rewiring and selective pattern execution, a branch less concerned with bodies than with behavior, which is how you get a program that doesn't just alter what someone's cells can do, but what someone will believe, and who they'll die for.

What he'd become, over those two years of rebuilding, deserved the same attention he would once have given a crime scene, because in the most literal sense, that's exactly what he'd spent his life investigating. His own body.

Start with the lattice. Somewhere inside that hospital room, years before he had the words for any of this, his cells had stopped behaving like cells. The ordinary double helix that holds a person together had reorganized itself into something else entirely — a dense, fortified lattice, built for one purpose: refusal. His cells refused to die. They refused to break down, refused ordinary illness, refused the slow decay every other body on earth quietly accepts as the price of being alive. In the narrowest clinical sense, it made him unkillable by anything the world calls natural.

The cost of that refusal is that his blood stopped being blood, in any sense a doctor would recognize.

Concrete is the material of the future. Fluorescent tubes and salvaged tools and old hardware nobody bothered replacing — not because anyone's being quaint about it, but because production itself stopped moving forward decades ago. The wealthy hoard what little genuine advancement still exists. Everyone else lives with whatever was left running.

Behind all of it sits one company. It has a name now — Rockcore Chemical Corp, RCC — though for a long time nobody outside its walls knew to call it anything. It isn't one villain among several. It's the single hand behind every catastrophe in this world, wearing four different faces so that no one has to notice it's the same hand each time.

RCC ran the corporate bio-arms race that got the world here. RCC quietly modified its own people — genetic upgrades, precise and deliberate, installed privately on the ownership class years before anyone else knew that kind of thing was even possible. The world would come to call these modifications "the cures," but that's a lie built into the language itself.

hello and welcome, today I’m presenting “The Whole of It” by Elijah Skinner.

I am a stranger in a land I did not build, carried by those who came before me, carrying those who will come after. I did not choose this. Not the life, not the waking, not the morning light casting its shadows without asking.

Humanity is one great continuous force — a canvas painted by every hand that ever was, each of us with a view too small to see the whole, each of us a mark inside something larger than the mark can comprehend. I did not choose to paint. I did not choose to collaborate. And those I bring into this world will not choose it either, nor will they receive a world without the limits others put in place before them.

Some mistake this for an insult and spend themselves demanding a different contract — the ego trip of choice, the delusion of separateness, the sense of power that comes from believing you stand outside the force rather than inside it. But to take without giving from a world that promised you nothing is not freedom. It is a misreading. A hand that believes smearing is the same as standing outside the canvas. It is not. There is no outside.

If the choice is only two options then only one can be right, and therefore the other is not a choice at all — it is only cruelty, and cruelty is not freedom, it is simply being wrong about what you are.

I do not envy control. I do not grieve consent. Beauty does not ask my permission and I will not pretend it should. What I have is not choice — it is inevitability dressed in attention. I cannot choose what I leave but I can leave something. I will give it my strength, my tending, the quiet propagation of fields I did not plant.

Because beauty only exists today because someone tended to it before I could choose it.

This is not tragedy. This is the terms.

 

And yet the terms do not end at the threshold of the exterior world. They follow me inward. They follow me all the way to the end.

I will not choose how I die. I will not choose how I am remembered. I cannot choose how I am buried. The entirety of an existence is assembled from choices that were never mine — not the arrival, not the departure, not what remains after.

Some fear this. They dissolve themselves against it — unmade by the premise rather than carried by it. But I do not have to believe a thing for it to be true. If belief were the requirement it would not be nature, only theory. The unchosen life does not wait for consent.

Look inward long enough and something stranger surfaces. The choices I do hold — I spend them poorly. I choose against myself. I choose in ways a more patient version of myself would not recognize, would turn from. The agency I guard so closely does not survive examination. It is impulsive. It is small. In many ways it exists only as a story I tell to feel less carried.

What remains when the story collapses is not emptiness — it is morning, and the work in front of me. There is still the hour, still the hand, still the crude and available day. Do not waste what little you are given.

 

What I do with my life is intricate, well-knit design. What I do with my days is the crude brick and mortar work of my experiences.

One day does not seem like much. But there are no grand cathedrals without all of the dragging days in between — the days of repetition without revelation, of tending without seeing growth, of hands that work without knowing what they are building toward. Each small reaction to each small day — the choice to tend rather than take, to add rather than consume — is not a grand gesture. It is mortar. It is the unglamorous material of a life accumulating into something that can finally be seen only from a distance, only by those who come after.

This is where the imagination lands. Not in chosen outcomes or grand interior revelations but in the return to the day. The reaction chosen in the small hours. The tending that asks nothing back. Because reaction chosen daily becomes habit, and habit becomes character, and character over a lifetime becomes the result I can finally rest with — the only architecture that was ever mine to build.

It is boring. It is necessary. It is simply your attention that grows beauty.

Not your agency. Not your consent. Not your understanding of the whole canvas or your place within it. Only your attention, returned to the day, returned to the crude work, returned again and again until the dragging days become the cathedral and the cathedral becomes what I leave for hands I will never know, who will not choose it either, and will not need to.

I was promised nothing.

I tend anyway.

That is not resignation.

Now build your cathedral.

“The Sixth Extinction”

Somewhere tonight, a species is disappearing that no one will ever name.

Not a war. Not a meteor. No fire in the sky to point to and say *there, that's the villain.* Just a slow closing door, one hinge at a time, and most of us in the next room, arguing about something else.

We are living inside the sixth extinction. The fifth one killed the dinosaurs. This one is killing everything, and we are the meteor. Not falling from the sky, walking on the ground, building, burning, paving, and calling it progress the whole way down.

I want to tell you what that actually looks like, because "extinction" is a word so big it stops meaning anything. So let me make it small again.

It looks like a frog that sang in one valley in Costa Rica, and only that valley, and doesn't sing anywhere anymore. It looks like the last of something dying not in a blaze but in a quiet corner while the rest of the world keeps its lights on. Species are vanishing now somewhere between one hundred and one thousand times the natural rate, and most of them go without a name, without a photograph, without a single person noticing the exact moment the world got a little more silent.

That should sit heavy in your chest. It should. I'm not here to talk you out of the grief. Grief is just love with nowhere left to go, and if you feel it when you think about a coral reef bleaching white or a forest turning to ash, that's not weakness, that's proof you're still paying attention.

But I didn't come up here just to make you carry weight. I came up here because I've watched something else be true, over and over, in my own life, in my own work — **a sealed system always dies, and a breathing system survives.**

Think about that. A jar with the lid screwed on tight doesn't preserve what's inside, it suffocates it. Every ecosystem that's collapsing right now is collapsing because we sealed it off — from movement, from connection, from the exchange that keeps a living thing alive. We drew borders through migration routes. We dammed the rivers. We built walls where there used to be corridors. We turned a breathing planet into a series of sealed rooms, and then we act surprised when the thing inside each room starts to die.

Here's the hope, and it's not a soft one, it's a working one: **nothing that still has breath in it is finished.** Every wolf reintroduced to a valley that changed the whole shape of a river. Every reef that came back once the water was given room to cool. Every species pulled back from the very edge of the list, not by luck, but by people who refused to accept the sealed version of the story.

We are not powerless here. That's the lie extinction wants you to believe — that this is weather, that this is fate, that it's already decided. It isn't. Somewhere right now a flock is still flying. We just forgot, some of us, which way is home.

So here's what I'm asking. Not for guilt. Guilt is a sealed system too, it just eats you instead of the planet. I'm asking for **breath.** Plant something native. Fight for the corridor, the wetland, the policy nobody else will read. Vote like the tide is still turning, because it is. Tell somebody the frog's name, even if you have to make it up, because the moment we start naming what we're losing is the moment we stop losing it quietly.

We didn't inherit a finished world. We inherited an unfinished one, mid-breath, and the question was never whether we could stop every door from closing. The question is whether we keep our hands on the ones still open.

Don't seal the room. Keep it breathing. Keep it breathing, and let that be the whole of your answer.
